usedCounterFrames: A complete pitch is not stronger because it includes every stage, but because no stage steals the next stage's job. Integration is rhythm: enough, then hand off.
A hookpoint is not a clever line, but an earned peak. If the room has not felt setup and consequence first, even the sharpest sentence lands like a slogan.
A pitch failure is not proof that the facts were weak, but evidence that the room stopped receiving them. Find that break before adding more proof.
Dense analysis is not the opener, but the second act. The first filter wants simple relevance, novelty, and threat before it lets careful proof earn attention.
Frame control is not louder confidence, but calmer interpretation control. The room may seem to be judging facts while it is actually judging the frame those facts have been placed inside.
Intrigue is not hiding information to look clever, but delaying the answer until the room has formed the right question. The reveal should satisfy curiosity tied to consequence.
Prizing is not acting unavailable, but making value conditional on real fit. The less needy stance comes from true standards, not from pretending the room should chase you.
STRONG is not a menu of clever moves but a pressure sequence. Each beat earns the next one before the room is asked to decide.
Story is not the long path to the point, but the shortest sequence that makes change and stakes visible. Background earns its place only when it moves the decision.
The reward is not swagger, but the ability to return to sequence under pressure. Confidence comes from controlled moves, not from a better mood.
Warm interest is not progress, but a place where delay can hide. The stronger move is to ask for the defined decision while the room still has energy to make it.
usedTryThisNowFrames: Map your current pitch as six one-line beats from frame to decision. Mark the beat you usually rush or skip.
Name the one moment where value, timing, and consequence should meet. Move any early fact that weakens that peak.
Open your last pitch and mark the first minute where proof appears before stakes. Replace that minute with one reason the room should care now.
Pick one fact you usually explain early. Write the question, pause, or visible test that would make the room ask for that fact first.
Put your pitch on one page as six timed beats. Cut the longest beat until the next handoff can happen without a reset.
Take one dense claim and rewrite it as one visible change, one risk, and one reason the listener should care before any detail appears.
Write a four-beat pitch path from first moment to final point. Delete any line that only proves effort.
Write one real constraint on your offer. Turn it into a fit question you can ask before price, timing, or commitment comes up.
Write the exact decision your next pitch needs: who decides, by when, and what calendar entry, form, or signature proves it happened.
Write the pressure moment most likely to make you chase approval, then name the STRONG beat you will return to instead.
Write the weak label the room may put on your offer. Beside it, write the decision frame you want judged before any detail appears.
